notes.definition: Addition polymerisation is the joining together of many small alkene molecules (monomers) to form a very large molecule (a polymer). The C=C double bonds open up and the monomers join in a chain; no other product is formed, so the repeating unit contains exactly the same atoms as the monomer.
explanation: Polymers are very large molecules made by joining many small molecules, called monomers, together. Alkenes can be used as monomers because they contain a C=C double bond. In addition polymerisation, the double bond in each monomer opens up (becomes a single bond) and each monomer bonds to the next one, forming a long chain. Thousands of monomers may join to make one polymer molecule. For example, many ethene molecules join to form poly(ethene), and many propene molecules join to form poly(propene).

In addition polymerisation the polymer is the only product: no other molecule, such as water, is formed. This means the repeating unit of the polymer has the same atoms as the monomer. For example, the monomer ethene is C₂H₄ and the repeating unit of poly(ethene) is also C₂H₄. We write the reaction as n C₂H₄ → (C₂H₄)ₙ, where n is a large number. The mass of polymer formed equals the mass of monomer used.

Polymers are drawn by showing one repeating unit inside brackets, with an 'n' outside to show it repeats many times. To draw the repeating unit from a monomer: draw the two carbon atoms that were in the double bond with a single bond between them, keep all the other atoms or groups attached to them in the same positions, and draw bonds sticking out on both sides through the brackets. These 'open' bonds show where the unit links to the next one.

To work out the monomer from a polymer, do the reverse: take the repeating unit, remove the bonds that extend through the brackets, and put a double bond between the two carbon atoms. The monomer must contain a C=C bond. Polymer names come from the monomer: poly(ethene) from ethene, poly(propene) from propene and poly(chloroethene) from chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl).

Addition polymers are useful because they are strong, flexible or rigid, unreactive and waterproof. Poly(ethene) is used for plastic bags and bottles, poly(propene) for crates and ropes, and poly(chloroethene) (PVC) for window frames and pipes. Because they are unreactive, many addition polymers are not biodegradable, which causes problems with disposal.
keyFacts: Polymers are very large molecules made from many small monomers.
Alkenes are monomers for addition polymers because they contain C=C.
In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond becomes a single C–C bond.
No other product is formed, so the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer.
General equation: n monomer → polymer, e.g. n C₂H₄ → (C₂H₄)ₙ.
Repeating units are drawn in brackets with an n and bonds extending through the brackets.
To find the monomer: remove the extending bonds and put back the C=C double bond.
Mass of polymer formed = mass of monomer used.

keyTerms.definition: A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer, such as ethene.
A very large molecule made from many monomers joined together in a chain.
Polymerisation in which alkene monomers join by opening their C=C double bonds, with no other product formed.
The section of a polymer chain that repeats; in addition polymers it has the same atoms as the monomer.
The addition polymer made from ethene monomers.
The addition polymer made from propene monomers.
Containing a C=C double bond; monomers for addition polymers must be unsaturated.

equations.name: Relative formula mass of an addition polymer
equations.formula: Mr of polymer = n × Mr of monomer

workedExamples.title: Drawing the repeating unit
workedExamples.question: Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl, forms poly(chloroethene). Describe how to draw the repeating unit.
steps: Draw the two carbon atoms joined by a single bond (the double bond has opened).
Keep the substituents in place: two H on the first carbon; one H and one Cl on the second carbon.
Draw a bond out from each carbon through the brackets, and write n after the closing bracket.
workedExamples.answer: –[CH₂–CHCl]ₙ–, a repeating unit containing C₂H₃Cl with bonds extending out of the brackets.

workedExamples.title: Finding the number of monomers
workedExamples.question: A poly(propene) molecule has Mr = 63 000. How many propene units are in it? (Mr of propene, C₃H₆ = 42)
steps: The repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer, so each unit has Mr = 42.

workedExamples.title: Identifying the monomer
workedExamples.question: A polymer has the repeating unit –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ–. Name the monomer.
steps: Remove the bonds through the brackets.
Put a double bond between the two carbons: CH₂=CH(CH₃).
This is CH₂=CHCH₃, which is propene.

diagrams.title: Monomers joining in a chain
diagrams.caption: When ethene molecules polymerise, the double bonds open and the carbon atoms join to form a long chain with only single bonds.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often draw the repeating unit with the double bond still present.
misconceptions.right: In fact the C=C becomes a single C–C bond in the polymer; only the monomer has the double bond.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think water is produced in addition polymerisation.
misconceptions.right: In fact addition polymerisation gives only one product, the polymer; condensation polymerisation is the type that releases small molecules.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget the bonds that extend through the brackets.
misconceptions.right: In fact these bonds are essential: they show the repeating unit is joined to the next one on each side.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'poly(ethene)' contains C=C bonds because it is made from ethene.
misconceptions.right: In fact poly(ethene) is saturated; it has only single bonds, like a very long alkane.

realWorld: Poly(ethene) is used for carrier bags, bottles and cling film.
Poly(propene) is used for crates, ropes, carpets and food containers because it is tough and flexible.
Poly(chloroethene), PVC, is used for window frames, drainpipes and insulation on electrical cables.
separateOnlyContent: All of this subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only; Combined Science does not cover polymerisation.
examTips: In a repeating unit always include: single C–C bond, brackets, n, and bonds extending through the brackets.
Check the repeating unit has exactly the same atoms as the monomer.
To spot an addition polymer's monomer, look for a C=C bond in it; no C=C means it cannot be an addition monomer.
Name the polymer by putting the monomer name in brackets after 'poly'.
summary: Alkenes join to make addition polymers.
The C=C opens up and monomers join in a long chain.
Only one product forms, so repeating unit = monomer atoms.
Draw the repeating unit in brackets with n and extending bonds.
Reverse the process to find the monomer.

questions.question:
Polymers are made by joining together many small molecules.
What are these small molecules called?
markScheme: 1 mark: monomers
questions.explanation: Monomers are the small building blocks of polymers.

questions.question: Which polymer is made from ethene?
markScheme: 1 mark: poly(ethene)
questions.explanation: The polymer is named after the monomer: ethene gives poly(ethene).

questions.question: Which type of compound can be used as a monomer in addition polymerisation?
markScheme: 1 mark: alkenes
questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation needs a C=C double bond, which alkenes have. Alkanes are saturated.

Ethene undergoes addition polymerisation.
What else is formed in this reaction?
options: Nothing else: the polymer is the only product
markScheme: 1 mark: nothing else / only the polymer
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation all the atoms of the monomers end up in the polymer.

What mass of poly(propene) is formed?
markScheme: 1 mark: 500 kg
questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation forms only one product, so all the mass of monomer ends up in the polymer.

Formula of propene = C₃H₆
markScheme: 1 mark: Mr of propene C₃H₆ = 42
questions.explanation: First find the Mr of propene (36 + 6 = 42), then divide the polymer Mr by it.

Calculate the number of carbon atoms in the main chain of this poly(ethene) molecule.
markScheme: 1 mark: each ethene adds 2 carbon atoms to the chain

1 mark: poly(propene): crates / ropes / carpets / containers

questions.question: Explain why the repeating unit of an addition polymer contains the same atoms as its monomer.
markScheme: 1 mark: the monomers join by opening the C=C double bond
1 mark: no other product / small molecule is formed, so no atoms are lost

Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl, and propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, are both used to make addition polymers.
Explain how addition polymers form from these monomers.

• how each repeating unit is related to its monomer
• how you could identify the monomer from the structure of a polymer.
markScheme: Indicative content: both monomers contain C=C, so are unsaturated alkenes or alkene derivatives; many monomers join; the C=C opens to a single C–C bond and monomers bond in a chain; no other product; poly(chloroethene) repeating unit –[CH₂–CHCl]ₙ–, formula C₂H₃Cl; poly(propene) repeating unit –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ–, formula C₃H₆; repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer; side groups (Cl, CH₃) stay attached; to find the monomer remove the extending bonds and replace the C–C between the two carbons with C=C; brackets and n show many repeats.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear explanation of addition polymerisation, both repeating units correct, the monomer relationship explained and a correct method for working backwards.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explanation with at least one correct repeating unit and some link to the monomer.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic statements about monomers joining.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Treat both monomers the same way: open the double bond, keep the side groups, and add brackets, n and extending bonds.

questions.question: Describe what happens to the C=C double bond in a monomer during addition polymerisation.
markScheme: 1 mark: it becomes a single C–C bond (opens up)
questions.explanation: The double bond opens so each carbon can bond to the neighbouring monomer.
